issues.legal_issue: A decree entered in a suit barred by limitation is not a nullity when the court had jurisdiction over the subject matter and the parties.
material_facts: The appellant argued that an earlier decree on a hypothecation bond was a nullity because the suit had been brought out of time.
The court that entered the earlier decree had jurisdiction over the subject matter and the parties.
The limitation objection was not established as a basis for treating that decree as void.
issues.conclusion: Even if the earlier suit was barred by limitation, the decree was not a nullity and could not be ignored in later litigation; the error had to be corrected through an appeal against that decree.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 3 of the Limitation Act, 1908, a court must take notice of limitation even if it is not pleaded. As explained in Maqbul Ahmad v. Onkar Pratap Narain Singh, that duty does not mean that failure to enforce limitation deprives the court of jurisdiction. A court with jurisdiction may decide an issue wrongly, and the resulting error of law must be corrected through the procedures provided by the Civil Procedure Code; an unchallenged erroneous decree remains effective.

rule.if: later_proceeding_challenges_prior_decree and court_had_subject_matter_jurisdiction and court_had_jurisdiction_over_parties and prior_decree_entered_despite_limitation_bar

predicates.later_proceeding_challenges_prior_decree: The proceeding seeks to avoid or disregard a decree entered in an earlier case.
predicates.court_had_subject_matter_jurisdiction: The court that entered the earlier decree had authority over the kind of dispute before it.
predicates.court_had_jurisdiction_over_parties: The court that entered the earlier decree had authority over the parties to that case.
predicates.prior_decree_entered_despite_limitation_: The court entered the earlier decree even though the suit was barred by limitation.

issues.definition: When a later proceeding challenges a prior decree, and the court had authority over the dispute and the parties, the decree remains effective even if the suit was time-barred.

issues.legal_issue: A limitation objection that presents a mixed question of fact and law and was not raised in the High Court cannot be raised for the first time in the Supreme Court.
material_facts: The appellant did not raise a sufficiently clear limitation plea in the trial court or the High Court.
The appellant did not raise the limitation point in the High Court in support of the trial court's decree.
The point raised in the Supreme Court depended on both facts and law, including when the suit was first instituted and how the limitation period should be computed.
issues.conclusion: The Supreme Court declined to allow the appellant to raise the limitation point for the first time before it.
issues.legal_principle: A mixed question of fact and law that was not raised in the High Court is not to be introduced for the first time in the Supreme Court, particularly where the omitted factual plea could have led to evidence or a record inquiry in the courts below.

predicates.supreme_court_appeal: The case is an appeal before the Supreme Court.
predicates.limitation_issue_mixed_fact_law: Deciding the limitation issue requires both factual findings and application of law.
predicates.limitation_issue_not_raised_in_high_cour: The party did not raise the limitation issue in the High Court.

issues.definition: In a Supreme Court appeal, a party cannot introduce a limitation issue requiring factual and legal determination if it was not raised in the High Court.

issues.legal_issue: A suit for recovery from a trespasser may be within time when the period during which a court-appointed receiver held the property is counted for the successful party.
material_facts: The court found that actual possession had been delivered through execution to the auction purchaser.
The appellant's later possession began as a trespass after that delivery.
During proceedings concerning disputed possession, the property was attached and held by a receiver until those proceedings ended.
The respondents brought the civil suit after the receiver's period of possession, and the appellant argued that the suit was out of time.
issues.conclusion: The receiver's possession enured for the benefit of the successful party, and counting that period made the respondents' suit timely.
issues.legal_principle: The possession of a receiver appointed during proceedings under section 145 of the Code of Criminal Procedure enures to the benefit of the party who succeeds in the ensuing civil dispute. Because actual delivery had previously been made to the auction purchaser and the appellant's later possession was by trespass, the suit was treated as one to evict a trespasser, not as a suit by an auction purchaser seeking recovery on the basis of an execution sale. The relevant limitation analysis included the receiver's period of possession under Article 142 of the Limitation Act, 1908.

predicates.civil_suit_to_recover_property_from_tres: The proceeding is a civil suit seeking recovery of property from a person whose possession is alleged to be wrongful.
predicates.prior_actual_court_delivery_to_claimant: A court officer actually delivered possession of the property to the claimant or the claimant's predecessor.
predicates.receiver_held_property_during_possession: A receiver held the property while a proceeding about possession was pending.
predicates.receiver_possession_enured_to_successful: The party who succeeded in the relevant dispute was entitled to the benefit of the receiver's possession.

issues.definition: A civil suit to recover property from a trespasser is timely when prior court delivery supports the claimant's title and the receiver's possession during a possession dispute counts for the successful party.

issues.legal_issue: An assignment of a secured right may be found sham and ineffective when the circumstances show that it was not intended to transfer the right.
material_facts: The purported assignee did not attempt to realise the amount secured by the hypothecation bond for many years after the purported assignment.
The assignor was deeply in debt when the assignment document was made.
The assignor obtained the document back after presenting it for registration, and there was no evidence that it was later handed to or accepted by the purported assignee.
There was no evidence that the debts said to form much of the consideration were actually due or that the stated money had been paid.
The appellant produced no person directly connected with the assignment or the execution proceedings to support the transaction.
issues.conclusion: The purported assignment was sham and bogus, so the hypothecation rights remained available for attachment and sale in execution.
issues.legal_principle: Whether a transaction is genuine may be inferred from its surrounding circumstances, including whether consideration was proved, whether the document was delivered or accepted, whether the purported assignee acted on the rights, and whether the transaction was consistent with the parties' conduct. The Court agreed with the High Court's inference that the assignment was not genuine.

rule.if: purported_assignment_of_secured_right and consideration_unproved and assignee_never_enforced_right and document_not_shown_delivered_or_accepted

predicates.purported_assignment_of_secured_right: A document purports to transfer a secured right from one person to another.
predicates.consideration_unproved: The evidence does not establish that the consideration stated for the transfer was actually paid or due.
predicates.assignee_never_enforced_right: The purported assignee did not act to realise or enforce the transferred right over a lengthy period.
predicates.document_not_shown_delivered_or_accepted: The evidence does not show that the transfer document was delivered to or accepted by the purported assignee.

issues.definition: A purported assignment is treated as sham and ineffective when its consideration and completion are unproved and the purported assignee does not enforce the right.

issues.legal_issue: A purported sale between family members may be found sham when the stated consideration is unsupported and the seller continues to exercise ownership.
material_facts: The purported sale was from a father to his son, who was not shown to have independent means to provide the stated consideration.
The alleged payments were supported only by the son's testimony, and the stated sources of funds were inconsistent with his account in another proceeding.
A person said to have lent part of the consideration was a young child at the time.
Although the son claimed possession, the evidence supported the finding that he possessed the properties as his father's agent.
issues.conclusion: The purported sale was sham and bogus, and the son did not acquire rights under it.
issues.legal_principle: The genuineness of a conveyance is determined from the evidence and surrounding circumstances, including the purchaser's ability to provide the consideration, proof of payment, consistency of the parties' accounts, and the nature of the purchaser's possession. The Court upheld the finding that the stated consideration was not credible and that possession was consistent with agency rather than ownership.

rule.if: purported_family_sale and purchaser_lacked_independent_means and consideration_unproved and purchaser_possession_consistent_with_agency

predicates.purported_family_sale: A document purports to sell property between members of the same family.
predicates.purchaser_lacked_independent_means: The purchaser was not shown to have independent resources to provide the stated consideration.
predicates.consideration_unproved: The evidence does not establish that the stated consideration was actually paid or otherwise provided.
predicates.purchaser_possession_consistent_with_age: The purchaser's possession is consistent with holding the property on the seller's behalf rather than as owner.

issues.definition: A purported family sale transfers no rights when the purchaser lacks demonstrated means, the consideration is unproved, and the purchaser's possession is consistent with acting for the seller.

issues.legal_issue: A party has no vested right to have an appeal heard by a specified number of judges when the governing tribunal or its procedure has changed under competent legislation.
material_facts: The appeal was heard by a two-judge bench of the successor High Court rather than by a three-judge bench under the former High Court's law.
The former High Court had been abolished and a successor High Court established after the merger of the states.

The legislation governing appeals in the successor High Court replaced the earlier provisions, and the provision requiring a full bench for the relevant category had been repealed before the appeal was filed.
The appellant did not contend that the repeal was unconstitutional.
issues.conclusion: The appeal was rightly heard and decided by a two-judge bench; the appellant had no vested right to a bench of three judges.
issues.legal_principle: A right of appeal may be affected by competent legislation, and a litigant has no right to prevent abolition of the tribunal that existed when the suit was instituted. The right to appeal to a High Court does not confer a vested right to have the appeal heard by a specified number of judges; the composition of the bench is procedural. The Court relied on the legislation governing the successor High Court and noted that the repeal had not been challenged as unconstitutional.

rule.if: appeal_to_successor_high_court and former_tribunal_abolished_by_competent_law and bench_composition_is_procedural and no_vested_right_to_specific_bench

predicates.appeal_to_successor_high_court: The proceeding is an appeal before a High Court established as the successor to an earlier tribunal.
predicates.former_tribunal_abolished_by_competent_l: Competent legislation abolished the tribunal that existed when the original suit was instituted.
predicates.bench_composition_is_procedural: The number of judges assigned to hear the appeal is a matter of procedure.
predicates.no_vested_right_to_specific_bench: The party has no vested right to have the appeal heard by a particular number of judges.

issues.definition: An appeal before a successor High Court is validly heard by its authorised bench when competent law has replaced the earlier tribunal and procedure does not give the party a vested right to a particular bench size.
